The Western grey kangaroo (Macropus fuliginosus) exhibits a protracted developmental trajectory typical of large macropodids. Field studies indicate that the tiny neonate, weighing a mere 0.8343 grams [Wwb = 0.8343 grams] at parturition, climbs unaided to the pouch where it attaches permanently to a teat. This remarkably altricial offspring, born after a gestation period of approximately 35.6 days [tg = approximately 35.6 days] under a maternal body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], represents one of the most extreme examples of developmental immaturity at birth among eutherian mammals, though it is standard for marsupials. The mother’s investment during this early phase is exclusively through lactation, as the joey receives all its nourishment from milk while remaining continuously attached for the first several months. The physiological cost of sustaining this lactation is substantial; the average yearly milk production for an adult female has been calculated at roughly 201,732 joules per day  when measured at the typical active body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a figure that underscores the high energetic burden of rearing a single offspring through its lengthy pouch life.

The pace of development in Macropus fuliginosus is comparatively slow when set against smaller macropodids. The age at which the young permanently exits the pouch, a process known as weaning, has been documented as occurring around 320 days [tx = around 320 days] after birth at a maternal core temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This extended period of pouch dependency is consistent with the species’ large adult body size, as the weaning mass of the juvenile at this stage reaches approximately 6,500 grams (6500 grams) [Wwx = 6500 grams]. The time to permanent pouch exit reported here, gathered from longitudinal field observations of tagged individuals, aligns closely with the 319-day average described for the closely related eastern grey kangaroo. Following pouch exit, the young animal continues to suckle intermittently for several more weeks, gradually transitioning to a herbivorous diet composed primarily of grasses and forbs. This prolonged nutritional dependence likely reflects the poor quality of the forage available in the semi-arid and Mediterranean-type habitats the species occupies.

Sexual maturation in the western grey kangaroo is not achieved until well after weaning, marking a life history notable for its extended juvenile phase. Estimates for the time since birth at puberty show considerable individual variation, with the earliest recorded age at which all teats are everted in females being 670 days [tp = 670 days] when measured at a body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. However, a more typical value for the attainment of full reproductive capability is approximately 880 days [tp = approximately 880 days] after birth under the same thermal conditio at a temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]ns. This range, spanning from about 429 to 949 days in the published literature, reflects the strong influence of environmental quality—particularly rainfall-driven pasture productivity—on growth rates and the onset of puberty. The wide window for sexual maturity contrasts with the more tightly constrained timing observed in smaller macropodids and is likely an adaptive response to the unpredictable resources of the Australian interior.

The body mass trajectory of Macropus fuliginosus provides additional insight into its relatively slow life history. The wet weight at puberty, reflecting the somatic threshold required to initiate reproductive activity, averages around 16,500 grams (16500 grams) [Wwp = 16500 grams]. This represents less than half the ultimate wet weight that a fully grown adult can attain in high-quality habitat, as the maximum recorded body mass for the species is approximately 35,400 grams (35400 grams) [Wwi = 35400 grams]. Such a substantial difference between pubertal and asymptotic mass indicates that females continue to invest significantly in structural growth well after they become reproductively competent. In many populations, females do not breed in their first year of maturity, instead directing available energy toward reaching a more optimal body size that enhances both fecundity and offspring survival. This pattern of delayed reproductive effort in favor of continued somatic gain is common among large, long-lived herbivores and is especially pronounced in species inhabiting seasonally arid environments.

The lifespan of Macropus fuliginosus is among the longest recorded for any kangaroo species, reflecting its slow pace of life. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at just over 23 years [am = just over 23 years], when assessed at the species’ typical active body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with a low maximum reproductive rate, underscores a demographic strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity. The maximum reproductive output for the species is one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year] when measured at the same body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This extremely low fecundity is balanced by high juvenile survival in favorable years, with females capable of producing a single, well-provisioned young annually. The conservative reproductive strategy appears tightly linked to the constraints of lactational energetics and the unpredictability of forage resources in its distributional range.
